newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Saudi bourse looks cautiously at foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bourse looks cautiously at foreign investment.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is moving cautiously to open its bourse to foreign investors and has no immediate plans to link with other Gulf Arab stock markets, the kingdom's central bank governor said on Saturday.

"There are concerns about hot money coming in and going out. These considerations are to be considered and looked at first before giving full allowance for foreign investment," said Hamad Saud al-Sayyari, Governor of the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency.

"We are cautious concerning the disruptions that could happen. Money that would come and go quickly. That would cause the investor to be concerned or nervous and withdraw. That could cause the market to go up or down suddenly," he told Reuters.
Al-Sayyari did not say when the Saudi bourse, the biggest in the Gulf, would open its doors to foreign investment.

"It's difficult to give a time frame. I cannot say five or ten years, or two years. But the positive aspects are looked at and the negative aspects are looked at and it depends on weighing these," he said.
He was speaking on the sidelines of a Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) banking conference in Manama.
One of the issues raised at the conference was the possibility of merging Gulf Arab stock markets as a mechanism to encourage investment in the bourses.
Al-Sayyari said such measures were not on the Saudi agenda at this time.

"It is not a priority at the moment. But this is part of the overall development of the planned GCC market development. At the moment there is a linkage between Bahrain and Oman and there are no activities," he said.
"Investors, with the development of communications and services...can tap any market anywhere in the world without necessarily having a direct link," al-Sayyari added.

Bahrain and Oman in March 1995 began cross-listing shares in the first such step in the Gulf. In May, Bahrain, Oman and Kuwait said they planned to link their bourses to stimulate investment in publicly traded firms and financial instruments.

Bahraini, Kuwaiti and Omani bourses are open to investors in the GCC, which also includes Saudi Arabia, Qatar and United Arab Emirates. Some Bahraini and Oman firms are also open to foreign investors.

Saudi Arabia has been studying ways to boost liquidity on its stock market, with 70 listed firms capitalised at some $42 billion, including a wider range of financial instruments and foreign participation, according to bankers.

Only Saudi nationals can hold shares in all local firms. Nationals of other GCC states can own Saudi equities, excluding banks -- which account for about a third of market capitalisation -- and certain other stocks.
Analysts expect the first step towards allowing foreigners on the market will be through mutual funds. Of the 65 funds n the kingdom, eight invest solely in Saudi equities.
